# MinAI - Zero Dependency OpenAI Client for Java
A minimal Java client for OpenAI Chat Completions using only the JDK. No external dependencies.
## Why Zero Dependencies?
**Security & Trust** - No hidden CVEs in transitive dependencies - Smaller attack surface - only trust the JDK - No supply chain risks from third-party packages
**Simplicity** - No version conflicts with your existing libraries - ~15 KB vs 3-5 MB for typical clients - Perfect for serverless/containers (faster cold starts) - No dependency hell in shaded JARs or plugins
**Control** - You own the code - fix bugs immediately - No forced upgrades when libraries break APIs - Java's `HttpClient` won't disappear like third-party libs can
**Use Cases:** AWS Lambda, IntelliJ plugins, microservices, embedded apps, strict security policies
**Not For:** Streaming, function calling, vision, embeddings, or teams needing rapid prototyping
## Quick Start
### 1. Build
```bash mvn clean package ```
### 2. Usage
```java import io.github.vishalmysore.OpenAiCaller;
public class Example { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String apiKey = System.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"); String baseUrl = "https://api.openai.com/v1"; String model = "gpt-4o-mini";
OpenAiCaller caller = new OpenAiCaller(apiKey, model, baseUrl);
// Simple text completion with default temperature (0.7) String response = caller.generateCompletion( "You are a helpful assistant.", "Explain zero dependencies in one sentence." ); System.out.println(response);
// Custom temperature for more creative responses String creative = caller.generateCompletion( "You are a creative writer.", "Write a haiku about Java.", 1.2 // higher = more random/creative ); System.out.println(creative);
// Get full JSON response (includes token usage, model info, etc.) String fullJson = caller.getFullResponse( "You are a helpful assistant.", "What is the capital of France?" ); System.out.println(fullJson); } } ```
### 3. Run
```bash # Set your API key export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
# Run (no external JARs needed!) java -cp target/classes io.github.vishalmysore.OpenAiCaller ```
## Architecture
### Design Principles
1. **Use JDK APIs only** - `java.net.http.HttpClient` for HTTP, manual string building for JSON 2. **Fail fast** - throw exceptions on errors instead of silent failures 3. **No magic** - explicit, readable code over clever abstractions 4. **Separation of concerns** - domain objects (`Message`, `ChatCompletionRequest`) separate from HTTP logic
### Project Structure
``` src/main/java/io/github/vishalmysore/ ├── OpenAiCaller.java # Main HTTP client ├── Message.java # Simple message POJO ├── ChatCompletionRequest.java # Request builder with manual JSON serialization └── ChatCompletionResponse.java # Simple string-based JSON extractor ```
### How JSON is Handled
**Serialization (request):** ```java // Manual string building in ChatCompletionRequest.toJson() return "{" + "\"model\":\"" + escape(model) + "\"," + "\"temperature\":" + temperature + "," + "\"messages\":[" + messagesJson + "]" + "}"; ```
**Deserialization (response):** ```java // Simple string search in ChatCompletionResponse.extractFirstMessageContent() // Finds: "choices" → first "[" → "message" → "content":"..." // Then reads the string value character-by-character, handling escapes ```
This is intentionally simple and only handles the specific OpenAI response format. It's not a general JSON parser.
## Trade-offs
| Aspect | Zero Dependencies | With Libraries (Jackson + OkHttp) | |--------|------------------|----------------------------------| | **JAR size** | ~15 KB | ~3-5 MB (with transitive deps) | | **Security surface** | JDK only | 10+ libraries to audit | | **Dependency conflicts** | None | Common in large projects | | **Feature completeness** | Basic chat only | Full API support, streaming, etc. | | **Code complexity** | Higher (manual JSON) | Lower (library handles it) | | **Performance** | Comparable | Comparable (slightly faster for complex JSON) | | **Learning curve** | Steeper | Easier | | **Maintenance** | You own all code | Rely on upstream maintainers |
## Comparison: Dependency Count
**This library:** ```xml <dependencies> <!-- None! --> </dependencies> ```
**Typical OpenAI client (e.g., using Jackson + OkHttp):** ```xml <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>com.squareup.okhttp3</groupId> <artifactId>okhttp</artifactId> <!-- Pulls in: okio, kotlin-stdlib, kotlin-stdlib-common, annotations --> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId> <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId> <!-- Pulls in: jackson-core, jackson-annotations --> </dependency> </dependencies> <!-- Total: 7+ JARs, ~4 MB --> ```
**Popular OpenAI SDK (e.g., official or community):** - Can pull in 15-30+ transitive dependencies - Includes HTTP client, JSON parser, logging framework, annotation processors, etc. - Total size: 10-20 MB+
## Real-World Use Cases
### 1. AWS Lambda Function ```java // Cold start: ~200ms (vs ~800ms with heavy dependencies) public class LambdaHandler implements RequestHandler<Map<String, String>, String> { private static final OpenAiCaller CALLER = new OpenAiCaller( System.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"), "gpt-4o-mini", "https://api.openai.com/v1" );
@Override public String handleRequest(Map<String, String> input, Context context) { try { return CALLER.generateCompletion( "You are a helpful assistant.", input.get("query") ); } catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } } } ```
### 2. IntelliJ IDEA Plugin ```java // No dependency conflicts with the IDE's own libraries public class AIAssistantAction extends AnAction { @Override public void actionPerformed(AnActionEvent e) { OpenAiCaller caller = new OpenAiCaller(apiKey, model, baseUrl); String code = caller.generateCompletion( "You are a code assistant.", "Refactor this method: " + selectedText, 0.3 // lower temperature for more deterministic code ); // Insert into editor... } } ```
### 3. Docker Container ```dockerfile FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine # Tiny base image + single JAR = ~150 MB total COPY target/minai-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar /app.jar CMD ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"] ```
## Requirements
- **Java 11+** (for `java.net.http.HttpClient`) - **Maven** (for building, but no runtime dependencies) - **OpenAI API key** or compatible endpoint
## Configuration
### Using OpenAI ```java String apiKey = System.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"); String baseUrl = "https://api.openai.com/v1"; String model = "gpt-4o-mini"; // or "gpt-4", "gpt-3.5-turbo", etc. ```
### Using Azure OpenAI ```java String apiKey = System.getenv("AZURE_OPENAI_KEY"); String baseUrl = "https://YOUR-RESOURCE.openai.azure.com/openai/deployments/YOUR-DEPLOYMENT"; String model = "gpt-4"; // Azure uses deployment names // Note: Azure may require different header format - see Azure docs ```
### Using Local/Proxy Endpoints ```java String apiKey = "demo"; // or any placeholder String baseUrl = "http://localhost:8080/v1"; // LM Studio, Ollama, etc. String model = "llama-3.2"; // whatever your local model is called ```
## License
This project is released into the public domain. Do whatever you want with it.
## Contributing
This project intentionally has no dependencies. Pull requests that add dependencies will be rejected.
Acceptable contributions: - Bug fixes in the manual JSON handling - Additional HTTP error handling - Support for more OpenAI parameters (max_tokens, top_p, etc.) - Better documentation - Performance improvements
Not acceptable: - Adding Jackson, Gson, or any JSON library - Adding OkHttp, Apache HttpClient, or any HTTP library - Adding logging frameworks (use `System.out`/`System.err`)
## FAQ
**Q: Why not just use the official OpenAI Java SDK?** A: The official SDK is excellent and feature-complete, but it pulls in many dependencies. Use it if you need full API coverage. Use this if you need minimal dependencies.
**Q: Is manual JSON parsing safe?** A: For the specific OpenAI response format, yes. This isn't a general JSON parser—it's tailored to the known structure. Don't use this approach for arbitrary JSON.
**Q: What about streaming responses?** A: Not supported. Streaming requires SSE parsing which adds complexity. Use a full SDK if you need streaming.
**Q: Performance compared to Jackson?** A: For small payloads (typical chat completions), the difference is negligible (~1-2ms). Jackson wins for very large/complex JSON.
**Q: Can I use this in production?** A: Yes, if your use case fits (simple chat completions, no streaming, no function calling). Many production systems value simplicity over features.
**Q: What if OpenAI changes their API?** A: You own the code—update it yourself. This is actually an advantage: you're not waiting for a library maintainer to release a patch.
## Alternatives
If this doesn't fit your needs, consider:
- **[OpenAI Java SDK](https://github.com/openai/openai-java)** - Official, full-featured, well-maintained - **[LangChain4j](https://github.com/langchain4j/langchain4j)** - Powerful framework for LLM apps - **[Simple OpenAI](https://github.com/sashirestela/simple-openai)** - Good middle ground with fewer deps
## Support
This is a minimal educational/utility project. There's no official support, but: - Open an issue for bugs - Read the code (it's short!) - Fork it and customize for your needs
---
**Built with ❤️ and zero dependencies.**

# MinAI - Zero Dependency OpenAI Client for Java
A lightweight, zero-dependency Java client for OpenAI's Chat Completion API that uses only the JDK.
## Why Zero Dependencies?
### 1. **Minimal Attack Surface**
Every external dependency is a potential security vulnerability: - **No transitive dependencies** means no hidden CVEs in libraries you didn't even know you were using - **Fewer attack vectors** - you only trust the JDK, which is already required and vetted - **Easier security audits** - review ~500 lines of code instead of thousands across multiple libraries - **No supply chain risks** - no risk of compromised packages from Maven Central or malicious maintainers
### 2. **Dependency Hell Avoidance**
Zero dependencies means: - **No version conflicts** - never clash with Jackson, OkHttp, or other libraries your application uses - **No transitive dependency explosions** - a typical "lightweight" HTTP client can pull in 10+ transitive dependencies - **No breaking changes** from library updates you don't control - **Perfect for libraries** - if you're building a library/framework, you won't force dependency choices on your users
### 3. **Startup Performance**
- **Faster classloading** - no scanning/loading of external JARs - **Smaller classpath** - relevant for containerized applications and serverless functions - **Reduced JVM warmup time** - fewer classes to JIT compile - **Lower memory footprint** - no overhead from unused library features
### 4. **Deployment Simplicity**
- **Single JAR deployment** - your compiled code is all you need (plus the JDK) - **Smaller Docker images** - every MB matters in container environments - **Faster CI/CD pipelines** - no dependency resolution or downloading - **No dependency conflicts in shaded JARs** - perfect for plugins, agents, or embedded scenarios
### 5. **Long-Term Maintainability**
- **No forced upgrades** - libraries deprecate features, change APIs, or go unmaintained - **Code you control** - fix bugs or add features without waiting for upstream maintainers - **Stable over years** - JDK HTTP client (`java.net.http`) is part of the platform and won't disappear - **Educational value** - understand exactly how HTTP and JSON work instead of relying on "magic"
### 6. **Regulatory & Compliance**
For some environments: - **License compliance is simpler** - only your code + JDK license, no Apache/MIT/BSD license tracking - **Easier SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) generation** - fewer components to document - **Meets "no third-party code" requirements** in certain government/enterprise settings
## When Should You Use This?
✅ **Good fit for:** - Microservices where you only need basic OpenAI chat completions - AWS Lambda / serverless functions (cold start optimization) - Embedded applications, plugins, or agents - Educational projects or learning how APIs work - Security-sensitive environments with strict dependency policies - Libraries that don't want to impose dependencies on users
❌ **Not recommended for:** - Complex use cases needing streaming, function calling, vision, embeddings, etc. - Applications already heavily using Jackson/OkHttp (no benefit to avoiding them) - Teams unfamiliar with manual JSON handling (higher bug risk) - Rapid prototyping where developer velocity matters more than dependencies
## What's Included
- ✅ OpenAI Chat Completions API support - ✅ System and user messages - ✅ Configurable temperature - ✅ Manual JSON serialization (no Jackson) - ✅ Java 11+ HttpClient (no OkHttp) - ✅ Error handling and status code validation - ✅ Support for any OpenAI-compatible API (OpenAI, Azure, local proxies)
## What's NOT Included
- ❌ Streaming responses - ❌ Function calling / tools - ❌ Vision (image inputs) - ❌ Embeddings API - ❌ Audio/TTS/Whisper - ❌ Assistants API - ❌ Robust JSON parsing (uses simple string operations) - ❌ Retry logic with exponential backoff - ❌ Request/response logging frameworks
